newsitem.title: USA: Fine autumn day gives Clinton perfect photo-op.
newsitem.headline: Fine autumn day gives Clinton perfect photo-op.

text.p: "OK, let's clear the set," said one of the photographers as a local resident strayed into his shot.

The scene was picture perfect -- a cool autumn day ablaze with leaves, a clear blue sky, the grass of the campus quadrangle still green with summer, and the main character waiting off-stage to make his entrance.
But this was neither a movie set nor an advertising photo shoot.

The protagonist was the president of the United States, the set carefully staged by his staff, and the scene simply a standard Saturday morning photo-op designed to get Bill Clinton on television and into the newspapers.
One day before his first presidential debate with Republican Bob Dole, the president was devoting himself single-mindedly to debate practice.

But he still took the time to drive a golf cart across the Chautauqua Institution, a coffee cup in his hand, to give the photographers, camera operators and journalists on the scene some words and images to broadcast around the world.
After filming his arrival at the main square of the Institution, a retreat in western New York state devoted to the arts and religion, the journalists were shepherded into a bookstore after Clinton.

Placed behind low stands of bookshelves, they were in position to video and photograph the president as he signed copies of his campaign book "Between Hope and History" and mingled with local residents.

Even the president joked about the absurdity of the scene, with a half dozen camera operators and photographers filming his chit-chat, a radio reporter and a stenographer recording his every word, and journalists jotting furiously in their notebooks.

After studiously ignoring the journalists, who are herded into such photo-ops at least once a day in this campaign season, he turned to the cluster of lenses trained on him and said with mock surprise: "You're all here!"
The journalists were then led back outside to the quadrangle and placed behind yellow police tape in position to throw questions at the president after he walked out of the book shop.
While the questions were the one element of the photo-op the White House staff could not control, Clinton's answers had been carefully scripted.

Walking up to the cameras with a humble "aw shucks" look on his face, the president continued to play down his debating skills in an old political game of trying to lower public expectations of his performance.
On Thursday he claimed to be "apprehensive" and on Friday he said that former Maine Senator George Mitchell, who was impersonating Dole in Clinton's practice sessions, had "beat me like a drum."
Asked on Saturday whether he had finally got the better of Mitchell, Clinton replied, "Well, I don't know. Maybe I got him to a draw."
This scene was set so that the president appeared surrounded by a blaze of red, yellow and orange autumnal leaves, with an elegant, Georgian-style red brick library behind him.

The White House puts much time and energy into crafting such images, in recent months using Yellowstone National Park, the Grand Canyon and even a cheese-steak sandwich stop in a working class Philadelphia neighbourhood as backdrops for the president.

Sunday night will provide one of the few moments in the campaign -- the first of two crucial face-to-face debates with his opponent Bob Dole -- where the White House does not have total control over the image-making.
By agreement of the two campaigns, the stage in the Hartford, Connecticut hall will be simple -- just two lecterns for the candidates and a lowered table facing them for the moderator.
